cd_definition_quote: From Funk & Owen-Smith (2017), Management Science 63(3):791-817, pp. 794-795, Eq. (1)-(3): "CD t = 1/n_t * sum_{i=1}^{n_t} [(-2 f_it b_it + f_it) w_it], w_it > 0" with "f_it = 1 if i cites the focal patent (type f), 0 otherwise" and "b_it = 1 if i cites any focal patent predecessors (type b), 0 otherwise", and "n_t is the number of forward citations of both the focal patent and/or its technological predecessors". Expanding the sum gives CD = (n_i - n_j) / (n_i + n_j + n_k), where n_i = only cites the focal work, n_j = cites both the focal work and its references, n_k = only cites its references.

cd_naming_in_wu2019.quote: Subsequent work may cite: (1) only the focal work (i, green), (2) only its references (k, black) or (3) both focal work and references (j, brown).
cd_naming_in_wu2019.source: Wu et al. 2019 Extended Data Fig. 5g legend, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-0941-9

five_year_window_source.quote: Most of our analyses in this and later sections evaluate impact and the CD t and mCD t indexes using forward citations made during the first five years after the focal patent's issue, because annual citations of most patents reach their peak within this time frame (Jaffe and Trajtenberg 2002). We denote these quantities as I5, CD 5, and mCD 5, respectively.
five_year_window_source.wu2019_usage: 5-year window is the main specification; Extended Data Fig. 3 d-h tests robustness for windows from 5 to 40 years on 166,310 WOS papers published in 1970, and i-m repeats it on 24,174,022 papers 1954-2014.

equivalence.verdict_qualification: Strict algebraic identity holding exactly when B = n_j + n_k (i.e. the implementation's minus-1 correction equals zero and the citation-count set is identical). If B differs from n_j + n_k the two expressions are only approximately equal; the script's 'B - 1' makes the strict form conditional.
derivation: A = n_i + n_j: every paper citing the focal work in the window either cites only the focal work (n_i) or also its references (n_j); the two classes are disjoint and exhaustive.
J = n_j: papers citing both the focal work and any of its references are exactly the n_j class.
B = n_j + n_k - k: if the raw count of papers citing any reference of the focal work is n_j + n_k, the script's B (= raw count - 1) equals n_j + n_k - k with k = 1.
Denominator with k = 0: A + B - J = (n_i + n_j) + (n_j + n_k) - n_j = n_i + n_j + n_k.
Combine: (A - 2J)/(A + B - J) = (n_i - n_j)/(n_i + n_j + n_k).
assumptions: The set of papers citing any reference of the focal work within the window is exactly the focal work's predecessor set used in the literature (same reference universe).
OpenAlex meta.count counts distinct works, not citation edges, and is unaffected by pagination.

The literature definition already deduplicates: b_it equals 1 if a paper cites ANY predecessor (Eq. 3), so a paper citing several references still counts once; the 'any reference' counting in the code matches this.

algorithmic_check.result: simplify((A-2J)/(A+B-J) - (ni-nj)/(ni+nj+nk)) == 0; denominator expands to ni + nj + nk

numeric_check.sampling: n_i, n_j, n_k drawn independently uniform integers in [0, 500]

minus_one_analysis.theory: Papers citing the focal work's references in the window are n_j or n_k; the focal work itself cannot cite its own references inside its own citation window, so subtracting 1 has no theoretical basis under the 'papers citing its references' definition.
minus_one_analysis.effect_formula: With B = n_j + n_k - k the script computes (n_i - n_j)/(n_i + n_j + n_k - k); identity holds only when k = 0.

replacing_B_with_B_plus_1.definition: delta = CD5(B) - CD5(B+1) = script value minus literature value, computed exactly with fractions.Fraction over all 320 rows

batch1_effect.note: No CD5 sign flips in any of the 320 papers. The bias is a small systematic POSITIVE shift: most rows shift by ~1e-8 (negligible), a few rows with tiny A and B shift by up to ~4.8e-2, lifting the mean to +1.49e-4; B is usually far larger than A so the denominator barely moves.

minus_one_analysis.impact_on_protocol_verdict: No effect on H1 sign-based verdict observed in batch1; still a measurable deviation from the literature definition at the individual-CD5 level.

conclusion_summary.direction: Negative with team size: larger teams tend to develop existing lines of work while smaller teams tend to disrupt.
conclusion_summary.quote: smaller teams have tended to disrupt science and technology with new ideas and opportunities, whereas larger teams have tended to develop existing ones
conclusion_summary.sample: more than 65 million papers, patents and software products, 1954-2014
explanations_given_by_authors: Larger teams build on more recent and popular developments and receive attention immediately.
Smaller teams search more deeply into the past, are seen as disruptive, and succeed further into the future, if at all.
Differences are magnified for higher-impact work.
Topic and research design explain only a small part; most of the effect occurs at the individual level as people move between team sizes.
Both team sizes are essential; policy should support a diversity of team sizes.
conclusion_summary.accounting_note: Funk & Owen-Smith (2017) report a small POSITIVE correlation between number of inventors and CD5 in patent data (r = 0.02, p < 0.001), i.e. opposite in sign to Wu et al.'s paper-based result; data type, window and sample differ, so do not transpose results across the two.
